title: Events
summary: An event is something that happens on a page, such as a click or a key press.
introduction: An event is something that happens on a page, such as a click or a key press. Tell a button what to do after a click. Then learn how the event tells your code which part of the page was used.
learningObjectives: Register and remove event listeners with addEventListener
Read the event object to find the target, the typed value or the pressed key
Prevent default actions such as form submission and link navigation
Handle events on many elements with one listener using delegation

blocks.text: `element.addEventListener(type, handler)` tells the browser to call `handler` every time an event of that `type` happens on the element. The handler is a function you pass *by reference*; the browser calls it later. You can add as many listeners as you like, to the same or different events. The example creates a button, listens for `click`, then calls `button.click()` twice to simulate a user so the output appears in the console.

blocks.title: Passing the call instead of the function
blocks.text: `button.addEventListener("click", showMenu())` runs `showMenu` immediately, once, while the listener is being registered, and registers its return value (usually `undefined`) as the handler. Pass the function itself: `showMenu`, or wrap it in an arrow when it needs arguments: `() => showMenu("main")`.

The browser passes an **event object** to the handler. `event.type` is the event name, `event.target` is the element where it happened, and specific events add their own properties: `input` events let you read `event.target.value`, keyboard events have `event.key`, mouse events have `clientX` and `clientY`. Here the events are dispatched from code with `dispatchEvent`, which is also how tests simulate users.

blocks.text: Many events have a built-in consequence: submitting a form sends it and reloads the page, clicking a link navigates. `event.preventDefault()` cancels that behaviour so your code can take over, which is how single-page apps submit forms without a reload. The `{ once: true }` option removes a listener automatically after its first call, and `removeEventListener` removes one by hand (it needs the same function reference you added).

blocks.text: After an event fires on an element it **bubbles**: it travels up through every ancestor, and listeners on those ancestors run too. That makes **event delegation** possible: instead of attaching a listener to each of a hundred list items, attach one to the list and use `event.target.closest("li")` to find which item was clicked. Items added later are handled automatically, because the listener lives on the parent.

blocks.text: Notice that the buttons have `type="button"`. Inside a form a button submits by default, so the attribute matters whenever a button should only run JavaScript; the [HTML forms](/tutorials/html/forms) lesson covers the three button types.

blocks.title: Keyboard users
blocks.text: A `click` listener on a `<button>` also fires when the user presses Enter or Space on it, so buttons are accessible for free. Avoid attaching click handlers to `<div>` or `<span>`: they cannot receive keyboard focus, so keyboard and screen-reader users cannot activate them.

questions.question: Which call stops a submitted form from reloading the page?
questions.explanation: preventDefault cancels the browser's built-in action for the event. stopPropagation only stops bubbling to ancestors; it does not affect the default action.

questions.question: A click listener on a `<ul>` also runs when one of its `<li>` children is clicked.
questions.explanation: Events bubble from the target up through its ancestors, so the list's listener runs for clicks on its items. That is what makes event delegation work.
